title: Facts and Interpretations
objective: After this level you can tell a historical fact from an interpretation, using historians' rival explanations of why the colonists rebelled.
summary: A fact can be checked; an interpretation argues why. Becker (1909) saw a fight over who should rule at home; Bailyn (1967) saw ideas and a fear of conspiracy against liberty.

cards.headline: Colonists hated the Stamp Act. Why they rebelled is another story.
cards.body: Historians share the same evidence and still disagree. This chapter is about how they argue, starting with the difference between a fact and an interpretation.

cards.headline: What happened, and why
cards.body: Start with something you can check. Remember Level 21? The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed newspapers, legal papers, pamphlets, playing cards and dice. That is a fact: the records prove it. Why colonists went from protesting a tax to fighting a war is an interpretation, an argument built out of facts. The study of how those arguments change over time has a name: historiography, the history of history writing.

cards.headline: Who should rule at home?
cards.body: In 1909 the historian Carl Becker saw two struggles at once. One was over home rule: the colonies against Britain. The other was over who should rule at home: ordinary colonists against their own elite. Progressive historians such as Becker and Charles Beard read the Revolution as a class struggle, and treated the fine speeches about liberty as largely a cover for interests. In their view, interests explained more than speeches.

cards.headline: Take the ideas seriously
cards.body: In 1967 Bernard Bailyn answered from the other side. He studied the pamphlets of the era and took the revolutionaries at their word, assuming people meant what they wrote. In The Ideological Origins of the American Revolution, he argued those ideas gave colonists a strong fear of tyranny and of conspiracies against their liberty. That fear, he said, explains why they reacted so hard to Britain’s new policies of the 1760s.

cards.headline: Same facts, rival stories
cards.body: Notice what Becker and Bailyn share: the same taxes, protests and pamphlets. They disagree about why people acted. So when you meet a claim about the past, ask one question first. Can I check this, or is someone arguing? Facts get checked. Interpretations get weighed, by how much of the evidence they explain.

mascot.line: Keep this one: a fact answers what happened. An interpretation answers why, and it is only as strong as its evidence.

cards.headline: Facts and Interpretations: explained
learned: A fact can be checked; an interpretation argues why
Becker: home rule and who should rule at home
Bailyn: ideas and fear of a plot against liberty
Historiography is the history of history writing

questions.prompt: In 1909, _____ argued that the Revolution was also a struggle over who should rule at home.

options.label: Bernard Bailyn
options.rationale: Bailyn wrote in 1967 about ideas and fear of conspiracy.

options.label: Thomas Paine
options.rationale: Paine wrote Common Sense in 1776, during the Revolution.

options.label: Matthew Josephson
options.rationale: Josephson wrote about Gilded Age tycoons, in 1934.

questions.explanation: Carl Becker argued in 1909 that the Revolution was about home rule and about who should rule at home.

questions.prompt: Match each historian or term with its idea.
questions.explanation: Carl Becker saw a second struggle over who should rule at home. Bernard Bailyn argued the colonists had a strong fear of tyranny, and historiography is the history of history writing.

questions.prompt: Stamp Act protesters argued they could be taxed only with their own consent. How would Bailyn treat that argument?

options.label: As a sincere belief that drove their resistance
As a cover for the interests of the elite
options.rationale: That is closer to the Progressive reading of Becker and Beard.

options.label: As an idea invented by Parliament
options.rationale: Parliament argued for virtual representation instead.

options.label: As unimportant, since the Stamp Act was repealed
options.rationale: Bailyn took the colonists’ ideas seriously as causes.

questions.explanation: Bailyn took the revolutionaries at their word, so their argument about consent was a real idea that shaped what they did.
